params.title: Transmitting Systems
params.subtitle: Synchronizer, modulator, PFN and magnetron; TR and ATR tubes and circulators; timers and power supplies.

onScreen: TR and ATR tubes, circulators, timers and power supplies
scenes.narration: This lesson follows a RADAR pulse from start to finish. RADAR stands for radio detection and ranging. First, we'll see how the synchronizer, the modulator, the pulse forming network and the magnetron produce each pulse. Then, how a pair of gas tubes, or a ferrite circulator, lets one antenna both transmit and receive. And finally, how the transmitter's power supplies work. Let's start with the transmitting system as a whole.

onScreen: Synchronizer: trigger pulses set the PRR
Display sweep started by the trigger
scenes.narration: Here's the transmitting system, block by block. The synchronizer generates a timing signal. Its trigger pulses establish the pulse repetition rate, or PRR. Each trigger fires the modulator and its pulse forming network, or PFN, which send high-voltage pulses of the proper shape and width to the magnetron. The magnetron is the RADAR's RF, or radio frequency, oscillator. When the modulator pulses it with high voltage, it oscillates for exactly that time, generating the output signal at the proper operating frequency, and that goes out to the antenna. The same trigger also starts the display sweep, keeping the whole system in step. And the power supplies feed the modulator.

params.title: Which block sets what?
rows: Trigger pulses that fire the modulator
Pulse width: a fixed discharge time
Not part of the transmitting system

onScreen: PFN: pulse width, a fixed discharge time
scenes.narration: Keep these pairings straight. The synchronizer sets the pulse repetition rate. The modulator provides high-voltage pulses of the proper shape and width; it does not set the repetition rate or tune the magnetron. The pulse forming network produces a pulse of the correct width. It's an artificial transmission line that charges between pulses, then discharges into the magnetron for a fixed time set by its inductors and capacitors. The magnetron sets the operating frequency. So the transmitting system is the modulator, its pulse forming network and the magnetron. A klystron is not part of it: where a marine RADAR uses one, it's the receiver's local oscillator.

params.title: Transmitter power supplies
items: Separate low voltage and high voltage supplies are normal
Low voltage supplies use switching circuits to deliver multiple voltages
Low voltage supplies may supply both AC and DC voltages
False: "high voltage supplies produce in excess of 5,000 volts AC"
RADAR high-voltage supplies deliver DC to charge the modulator

onScreen: Separate low and high voltage supplies
Low voltage: switching circuits, multiple voltages
False: in excess of 5,000 volts AC
scenes.narration: Now the power supplies. It's normal for a RADAR transmitter to have separate low voltage and high voltage supplies. The low voltage supplies use switching circuits to deliver multiple voltages, and they may supply both alternating current and direct current, AC and DC. The exam asks which statement about modern RADAR transmitter power supplies is false. The false one says high voltage supplies produce voltages in excess of 5,000 volts AC. That's wrong because RADAR high-voltage supplies deliver DC, which charges the modulator.

callouts.label: Cathode: high voltage arrives as a strongly negative pulse
Anode block: kept at ground potential
The anode body connects to the waveguide and the chassis
External permanent magnet: a diode that needs a magnetic field
Curved electron paths excite the resonant cavities

onScreen: Anode body joins waveguide and chassis
scenes.narration: Meet the magnetron. It's a type of diode that requires an external magnetic field, and it has only 2 elements: a cathode and an anode block. High voltage is applied to the cathode, as a strongly negative pulse. The anode block stays at ground. It forms the outer body of the tube and connects to the waveguide and the chassis. A permanent magnet outside the tube curves the electrons' paths, so they excite the resonant cavities.

params.title: Why the cathode goes negative
items: High voltage goes on the cathode as a negative pulse
So the anode can be operated at ground potential, for safety
The anode-to-cathode voltage is the same either way
The anode is the outer body, joined to the waveguide and chassis
At ground, the anode is still positive relative to the cathode

onScreen: Negative high voltage on the cathode
Anode still positive relative to the cathode
scenes.narration: Why put a negative voltage on the cathode, rather than a positive voltage on the anode? So that the anode can be operated at ground potential, for safety. The anode-to-cathode voltage is the same either way. The anode of a magnetron is normally kept at ground because it forms the outer body and connects to the waveguide and the chassis. And even at ground, the anode is still positive relative to the cathode, so the tube works just the same.

params.title: Rise time and range accuracy
labels: Range is timed from the pulse's leading edge
Fast, sharp rise: a precise starting reference
Slow rise: the timing point becomes uncertain

onScreen: Range timed from the leading edge
scenes.narration: The magnetron's output pulse has a rise time, and it relates to accurate range measurement. Range is timed from the pulse's leading edge. A fast, sharp rise gives a precise starting reference for that timing. A slow rise makes the timing point uncertain, so the measured range is less accurate. That's why you want a sharp rising edge, like the ones drawn here.

onScreen: Klystron: receiver's local oscillator in older sets
scenes.narration: Which device is used as the transmitter in a marine RADAR? The magnetron, because it efficiently produces high-power microwave pulses from a compact, rugged tube. Don't mix it up with its neighbors. The klystron served as the receiver's local oscillator in older sets. And the thyratron is a modulator switch: it discharges the pulse forming network, as we'll see next.

blocks.label: Trigger
blocks.note: From the synchronizer: only starts it

blocks.label: Pulse forming network
blocks.note: Its L and C set the pulse duration

onScreen: PFN's inductors and capacitors set the pulse duration
scenes.narration: Let's look inside the modulator. A trigger from the synchronizer fires the switch. In older sets the switch is a hydrogen thyratron; in solid-state sets it's an SCR, a silicon-controlled rectifier. Either one may act as the modulator, as the switching element. The switch feeds a step-up pulse transformer, which drives the magnetron cathode. Where does the energy come from? Between pulses, the high-voltage supply charges the pulse forming network. When the switch fires, it discharges the PFN into the pulse transformer. The PFN's inductors and capacitors set how long the discharge lasts. So in a solid-state modulator, the duration of the transmitted pulse is determined by the pulse forming network. The trigger only starts it.

params.title: Pulse modulation
labels: Brief high-voltage pulses switch the magnetron fully on and off
RF is emitted only in short bursts
Once per pulse: the modulation frequency is the PRR
For the exam: most RADAR systems, 60 to 500 Hz

onScreen: Magnetron switched fully on and off
scenes.narration: A PFN driving the magnetron cathode through a step-up transformer gives pulse modulation. Brief high-voltage pulses switch the magnetron fully on and off, so RF is emitted only in short bursts, with silence in between. The modulator fires the magnetron once per pulse, so the modulation frequency is simply the pulse repetition rate. For the exam, the modulation frequency of most RADAR systems is between 60 and 500 hertz.

params.title: The modulator's job
items: In a pulse modulated magnetron, the PFN sets pulse shape and width
The thyratron only acts as the switch that discharges the PFN
Purpose of the modulator: the correct waveform to the transmitter
A high-voltage pulse of correct amplitude, width and shape at each trigger
Bearing resolution and sea return depend on the antenna and receiver

onScreen: PFN sets pulse shape and width
Modulator: correct waveform to the transmitter
Not bearing resolution or sea return
scenes.narration: In a pulse modulated magnetron, the pulse forming network determines the shape and width of the pulse. The thyratron only acts as the switch that discharges it. So what is the purpose of the modulator? To provide the correct waveform to the transmitter: a high-voltage pulse of the correct amplitude, width and shape at each trigger. Bearing resolution and sea return are not its job; they depend on the antenna and the receiver. And when asked what may act as the modulator, pick the thyratron or the SCR. The magnetron and klystron are microwave oscillators, and the video amplifier belongs to the receiver.

params.title: The PFN: an artificial transmission line

onScreen: An artificial transmission line, or delay line
Component values fix the pulse shape and duration
scenes.narration: Here's the pulse forming network up close. Pulse forming networks are usually composed of series inductors and shunt capacitors. Along the top, a chain of series inductors leads to the output. From each section, a shunt capacitor drops down. This ladder imitates a real transmission line's series inductance and shunt capacitance, so the PFN is an artificial transmission line, also called an artificial delay line. It stores energy in its inductor and capacitor sections, then releases it as a nearly rectangular pulse. The shape and duration of the high-voltage pulse delivered to the magnetron are established by this delay line: its component values fix the pulse.

params.title: Charging the PFN, then the pulse
labels: Charging choke: PFN charges to nearly twice the supply voltage
A diode holds the charge until the switch fires
Discharge: a flat-topped pulse lasting twice the line's one-way delay
The PFN sets the pulse width; the synchronizer sets the PRR

onScreen: Charges to nearly twice the supply voltage
Flat-topped pulse, twice the one-way delay
scenes.narration: How can the modulator pulse have an amplitude greater than the supply voltage? By employing a resonant charging choke. The choke resonates with the PFN capacitance. As its magnetic field collapses, it keeps current flowing, so the capacitors charge to nearly twice the supply voltage. A diode holds them there until the switch fires. Then the PFN discharges, delivering a flat-topped pulse that lasts twice the line's one-way delay time. That's the purpose of the pulse forming network: to determine the width of the modulating pulses. The synchronizer, not the PFN, sets the pulse repetition rate.

params.title: Switches for the PFN
items: Most often used in pulse-forming circuits: SCRs and thyratrons
Latching switches that withstand high voltage
They carry very high peak current and turn on fast
They turn off once the PFN is discharged

onScreen: Very high peak current, fast turn-on
Turn off once the PFN is discharged
scenes.narration: Which switching devices are most often used in pulse-forming circuits? Silicon-controlled rectifiers and thyratrons. They are latching switches: once triggered, they stay on. They withstand high voltage, carry very high peak current and turn on fast. Then they turn off once the PFN is discharged, ready for the next charge.

onScreen: Receiver isolated during the pulse, gets the echoes
scenes.narration: A RADAR uses one antenna for both transmission and reception. The duplexer is the electronic switch that makes this possible. A ferrite circulator is most commonly used in the duplexer. During each pulse, its one-way coupling sends the magnetron's pulse to the antenna and isolates the receiver. Then it routes the incoming echoes from the antenna to the receiver. In the RF section, a circulator replaces the TR, or transmit-receive, cell and functions as a duplexer. It does the job otherwise done by TR and ATR tubes, ATR meaning anti-transmit-receive.

params.title: Ferrites and cavities
items: The ferrite in a circulator is used as a phase shifter
Its phase shift depends on the wave's direction of travel
So energy circles one way: transmitter → antenna → receiver
A circulator replaces the TR cell; not cooling, testing or antenna position
Circular cavity, flat ends: E-lines perpendicular to the end walls, parallel to the axis

onScreen: Cavity E-lines perpendicular to the end walls
scenes.narration: How does the circulator steer the energy? The ferrite material in it is used as a phase shifter. In a magnetic field, the ferrite shifts a wave's phase by different amounts depending on its direction of travel. That steers energy one way around the ports: transmitter to antenna, and antenna to receiver. Remember, the circulator replaces the TR cell; it has nothing to do with cooling, testing or antenna position. One more microwave fact. In a circular resonant cavity with flat ends, the electric field lines, or E-lines, are perpendicular to the end walls. They run straight from one flat end wall to the other, parallel to the cavity's axis.

params.title: Directional coupler: −30 dB
steps: A −30 dB coupler samples 1/1,000 of the line power
The meter at the coupler reads 100 mW

onScreen: −30 dB samples 1/1,000 of the line power
scenes.narration: A directional coupler samples a small part of the power in a line. One with an attenuation of minus 30 decibels samples 1 part in 1,000 of the line power, because 10 to the power of 30 over 10 equals 1,000. So if the meter at the coupler reads 100 milliwatts, the line carries 100 milliwatts times 1,000, or 100 watts.

params.title: Transmitting: TR and ATR both fire

onScreen: ATR fired: pulse passes to the antenna
TR fired: shorts the receiver input
Keep-alive voltage: TR fires almost instantly
scenes.narration: Without a circulator, the duplexer uses gas-filled TR and ATR tubes. When a pulse RADAR is radiating, both the TR and ATR tubes are energized: the magnetron's high-power pulse ionizes the gas in both. The ATR tube fires, so the pulse passes freely to the antenna. The TR tube fires too, shorting the receiver input. So the TR box protects the receiver from the strong RADAR pulse and mutes it while the transmitter is on, until the gas deionizes. To make that happen fast, a DC keep-alive voltage is applied to the TR tube. It partially ionizes the gas, making the tube more sensitive, so it fires almost instantly when the transmitter pulse arrives.

params.title: Receiving: echoes go to the mixer

onScreen: ATR unfired: blocks the transmitter branch
Echoes kept out of the magnetron
Echoes pass the TR tube to the mixer
scenes.narration: Between pulses, the RADAR listens, and weak echoes come in from the antenna. The ATR box prevents the received signal from entering the transmitter. Unfired between pulses, it blocks the transmitter branch. The ATR tube is located between the magnetron and the mixer, so echoes go to the mixer instead of being absorbed by the magnetron. Protecting and muting the receiver is the TR box's job, not the ATR's. Meanwhile the TR tube's gas has deionized, so the echoes pass through to the mixer. That's why the keep-alive voltage only partially ionizes the TR tube: full ionization all the time would short the receiver and block the echoes.

params.title: TR tube versus ATR tube
rows: Between the magnetron and the mixer
Fires: protects and mutes the receiver
Fires: pulse passes freely to the antenna
Unfired: keeps echoes out of the magnetron

onScreen: TR: transmit-receive, at the receiver input
Between pulses echoes reach the mixer
scenes.narration: Here's the side-by-side. TR stands for transmit-receive, and ATR for anti-transmit-receive. Where are they? The TR tube sits at the receiver input. The ATR tube sits between the magnetron and the mixer, in the transmitter branch. During the pulse, both fire. The TR tube protects the receiver and mutes it, and the ATR tube lets the pulse pass freely to the antenna. Between pulses, the TR tube's gas deionizes, so echoes reach the receiver, while the unfired ATR tube keeps echoes out of the magnetron. And the DC keep-alive voltage goes on the TR tube, not the ATR tube.

params.title: The triggering section starts it all

onScreen: Indicator sweep starts at the same moment
Range markers start with each pulse
scenes.narration: Operation of any RADAR system begins in the triggering section. Its trigger fires the modulator, which drives the magnetron, and at the same moment it starts the display sweep. This timer circuit determines the pulse repetition rate, by generating the trigger pulses that fire the modulator, and it starts the indicator sweep with each pulse. The triggering section is also known as the synchronizer, because its trigger pulses synchronize the modulator, the indicator sweep and the range-marker circuits, so they all start together with each transmitted pulse.

params.title: The timer: the RADAR's master clock
items: Determines the pulse repetition rate (PRR)
Determines the range markers
Provides blanking and unblanking signals for the CRT
Unblanking: beam on only during the active sweep, blanked in retrace

onScreen: Blanking and unblanking for the CRT
Beam on only during the active sweep
scenes.narration: The timer circuit is the RADAR's master clock, and it does all of these jobs. It determines the pulse repetition rate. It determines the range markers. And it provides blanking and unblanking signals for the CRT, the cathode ray tube. The unblanking pulses from the timer are sent to the CRT. They turn its electron beam on only during the active sweep, so echoes are visible, and leave it blanked during retrace.

params.title: Accurate timing pulses
labels: Fires once, then its own RC timing cuts it off
Very short, sharp, stable pulses with fast rise times

onScreen: Fires once, cut off by its RC timing
scenes.narration: Which circuit best provides accurate RADAR timing pulses? A single-swing blocking oscillator. It's a transformer-coupled circuit that fires once and is then cut off by its own R C timing, set by a resistor and a capacitor. The result is very short, sharp, stable pulses with fast rise times, just what the timer needs to keep everything in step.

blocks.label: DC supply
blocks.note: Only about half the pulse voltage

blocks.label: PFN
blocks.note: Charges to nearly twice the supply

onScreen: DC supply: about half the pulse voltage
PFN charges to nearly twice the supply
scenes.narration: Back to the high-voltage supply. An advantage of resonant charging is that it reduces the high-voltage power supply requirements. The charging choke resonates with the pulse forming network, so the PFN charges to nearly twice the DC supply voltage, and a diode holds it there. That means the supply needs to produce only about half the pulse voltage.

params.title: Pulse-width modulation
labels: PWM varies the switch's duty cycle to control the output voltage
The switching frequency stays fixed; the on-time changes
Load impedance decreases → more current → wider pulses
Less load current, or rising input or output voltage → narrower pulses

onScreen: Less load current or rising voltage: narrower pulses
scenes.narration: Now the switching power supplies in a modern RADAR. A pulse-width modulator, or PWM, varies the duty cycle of the regulator switch to control the output voltage. The switching frequency stays fixed, while the on-time in each cycle changes. In a fixed-frequency switching power supply, the pulse width increases when the load impedance decreases. The lower impedance draws more current and pulls the output down, so the pulses widen to make up for it. Less load current, or a rising input or output voltage, narrows the pulses instead.

params.title: Switching versus linear regulator
rows: Switch is fully on or fully off
Pass transistor burns the excess voltage
Much higher: often 80 to 90 percent or more
Lower: the excess is lost as heat

onScreen: Switching: fully on or fully off
Linear: excess voltage burned as heat
Switching efficiency often 80 to 90 percent or more
scenes.narration: A major reason to use a switching regulator instead of a linear regulator is much higher overall efficiency. The switching regulator's switch is either fully on or fully off, so it wastes very little power, and its efficiency often reaches 80 to 90 percent or more. A linear regulator burns the excess voltage as heat in its pass transistor.

params.title: The power MOSFET switch
items: FET on: like a pure resistor, a small R<sub>DS(on)</sub>, no junction voltage drop
FET off: like a mechanical relay with open contacts
High input impedance from its insulated gate
Failure mode: gate punch-through from excess gate voltage or static
Resists thermal runaway: on-resistance rises with temperature

onScreen: Off: like a relay with open contacts
scenes.narration: In a modern RADAR switching power supply, the switch can be an FET, a field-effect transistor. When the FET is on, it compares to a pure resistor: a small R sub D S on, with no junction voltage drop. When it's off, it compares to a mechanical relay with open contacts. A power MOSFET, a metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor, has a high input impedance from its insulated gate. Its failure mode can be gate punch-through, when excess gate voltage or static punctures the thin gate oxide. And it resists thermal runaway, because its on-resistance rises with temperature.
